claims.claim: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines provide @dp.expect, @dp.expect_or_drop and @dp.expect_or_fail in pyspark.pipelines.

concept_html:
A data contract states what a delivery must look like before it may enter silver: row count range, mandatory columns, weight total, unique keys, allowed categories, expected distributions. Your reference project keeps each contract as versioned JSON, such as nat_contract_v2.json.

Every check produces a structured result, never a sentence:

CheckName = str
Status = Literal["PASS", "WARN", "FAIL", "SKIP"]
Severity = Literal["CRITICAL", "HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CheckResult:
    check_name: CheckName
    status: Status
    severity: Severity
    expected: str
    actual: str

Records can be counted, stored in a Delta table, charted and compared across waves. A narrative such as "weights look a bit high" cannot.

Severity decides what happens next.

  • A failed CRITICAL check stops the pipeline: raise an exception, so the job fails and silver stays untouched. Row count out of range, null keys, duplicate keys and a weight total outside limits are CRITICAL.
  • A WARN logs the result and the run continues. Unexpected category values and distribution shifts are warnings: worth a look, not worth a missed report.

Evaluate every check first, store all the results, then decide. If you raise on the first failure, you learn about one problem per run.

Keep the contract in data and the logic in code. A new contract version changes JSON, not Python.

On Databricks, Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines offer the same idea declaratively: @dp.expect records violations, @dp.expect_or_drop removes violating rows, and @dp.expect_or_fail stops the update. Use them when your pipeline runs in that framework. The contract pattern here works in any job.

lines: from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal
Status = Literal["PASS", "WARN", "FAIL", "SKIP"]
Severity = Literal["CRITICAL", "HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"]
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CheckResult:
"""One contract check outcome, ready to store in the QA results table."""
check_name: str
status: Status
severity: Severity
expected: str
actual: str
class ContractViolation(Exception):
"""Raised when one or more CRITICAL checks fail."""
def critical_failures(results: list[CheckResult]) -> list[CheckResult]:
"""Failed checks with CRITICAL severity."""
return [r for r in results if r.status == "FAIL" and r.severity == "CRITICAL"]
def enforce(results: list[CheckResult]) -> None:
"""Raise once, listing every CRITICAL failure. WARN results pass through."""
failures = critical_failures(results)
if failures:
names = ", ".join(f"{r.check_name} (expected {r.expected}, got {r.actual})" for r in failures)
raise ContractViolation(f"{len(failures)} critical check(s) failed: {names}")

exercises.solution:
class ContractViolation(Exception):
    """Raised when one or more CRITICAL checks fail."""


def enforce(results: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[dict[str, str]]:
    """Act on contract results.

    Args:
        results: Every check result for one delivery.

    Returns:
        The WARN results, for logging.

    Raises:
        ContractViolation: If any CRITICAL check failed. The message names each one.
    """
    critical = [r for r in results if r["status"] == "FAIL" and r["severity"] == "CRITICAL"]
    if critical:
        names = ", ".join(f"{r['check_name']} (expected {r['expected']}, got {r['actual']})" for r in critical)
        raise ContractViolation(f"{len(critical)} critical check(s) failed: {names}")
    return [r for r in results if r["status"] == "WARN"]

title: Data contracts with severity levels and structured results
why_html:
A contract validator raises on the first failed check. A redelivery has a row count 2% below the minimum, so the run stops at check 1. The supplier fixes the count and resends. The next run stops at check 4, duplicate keys. The third run stops at check 6, a weight total outside the range. Three round trips with the supplier cost four days.

Evaluating every check, storing all results, and then raising once for all CRITICAL failures gives the supplier one complete list on the first day.
